AfriScan · Namibia · Secure your land from the air, remotely

Know what is changing inside your servitudes and licence areas in Namibia

We map the structures, excavations, cleared ground, tracks and vegetation change along your power lines, roads and railways and across mining, petroleum and green-hydrogen licence areas in Namibia, measure each one to your line or boundary and show what changed between dated surveys. Satellite first, your own drone imagery where you already fly, and a person reviews every result before it reaches you.

The rules behind the work Electricity Act 2007 · Electricity Safety Code 2009 · Roads Ordinance 1972 · Ribbon Development Ordinance 1960 · Minerals Act 1992 · Petroleum Act 1991 · Communal Land Reform Act 2002 · Environmental Management Act 2007 · NAMCAR Part 101

Already in your agreements and the law

The distances your register is measured against

Namibian wayleave agreements, road ordinances and licence laws already draw lines around your assets. A line only protects the asset if someone can see what stands inside it, and when it arrived.

Wayleaves · Electricity Safety Code

Power lines: widths by wayleave, clearances by the Code

Power-line servitude widths are set in wayleave agreements. For one new 400 kV line, NamPower’s published resettlement framework describes an 80 m servitude in which “no permanent structures other than the towers are allowed”, with a 12 m strip cleared of vegetation (NamPower, November 2023). The Electricity Safety Code sets minimum clearances between live conductors and structures, from 3.0 m up to 33 kV to 5.6 m at 400 kV (Table 1).

Roads Ordinance 1972 · Ribbon Development Ordinance 1960

Roads: a 60 m reserve and a 100 m building restriction

Trunk, main and district roads have a 60 m road reserve, 30 m either side of the centre line where the boundaries have not been set otherwise, and farm roads 30 m (Roads Ordinance, s.3). Along trunk, main and building restriction roads, no structure may be put up within 100 m of the centre line without written permission, with exceptions for urban areas, existing township erven and low fences (Ribbon Development Ordinance, s.8).

Minerals Act 1992 s.52 · Petroleum Act 1991 s.16

Mining and petroleum: 100 m and 300 m

Licence holders need the owner’s prior written permission before working within 100 m of “any spring, well, borehole, reservoir, dam, dipping-tank… kraal, building or any structure of whatever nature”, or within 300 m of a surveyed erf (Minerals Act, s.52; Petroleum Act, s.16). A dated register of what stands near the planned workings is where that conversation starts.

Communal Land Reform Act 2002

Communal land: rights, fences and land boards

On communal land, nobody may occupy or use land except under a right acquired under the Act (s.43), fences need authorisation (ss.18, 44), and a land board can grant occupational land rights for government and state-owned-enterprise projects (s.36A) (Communal Land Reform Act). Chiefs, traditional authorities and land boards decide; we give them and you one dated map of what stands on the land.

The Roads Act 4 of 2025, not yet in force, would keep the reserve widths and add a building restriction of 45 m from the centre line in township areas and 500 m around intersections with other roads and railways (s.38(5)). Until it commences, the 1960 and 1972 Ordinances apply.

What you receive

A dated register your wayleave, land and GIS teams can use

  • Each structure listed with an ID, its distance to your line or boundary, its band, its chainage and its coordinates, in WGS84 and in the route’s UTM zone.
  • Every 500 m rated high, medium or low for encroachment density, so your wayleave officers know which spans and farms to visit first. It is a count rule, not a safety rating.
  • New and removed structures between dated surveys, with fresh digging, cleared ground and new tracks, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views.
  • The imagery named, and dated where the source gives a date.
  • A PDF report with maps, the segment table, a view of each structure and the coordinate register, plus GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers and an interactive map file that opens in a browser, including in the field.

Works with the drones you already fly

Your orthophotos, our registers and change layers

Many utilities and mines already fly drones for inspection and mapping. The flying is rarely the bottleneck. Turning each campaign’s orthophotos into a list of what is new, where, and how close it is to the line or boundary is.

Send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs you already hold. We run the structure, change and corridor analysis on them, a person reviews every result, and you receive the register, the segment ratings and the GIS layers. Between your flights, dated satellite scenes, where they exist for the area, show what has changed since the last one.

Analysis of your own imagery

  • Drone orthophotos and satellite GeoTIFFs you already hold
  • The same register, rating and change layers as our own surveys
  • Satellite scenes between your flights
  • Results depend on your imagery’s resolution and quality; we check a sample before we commit

Imagery: yours, archive or new capture

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, cleared ground, excavations, tracks and vegetation. We do not identify, count or follow people, and satellites cannot see theft or vandalism. Whether a structure is lawful is for you, the land boards, the authorities and the courts to decide; evictions are for the courts. Our registers support your wayleave, compensation, community and legal processes; they do not replace any of them.

A person reviews every result

Building datasets and detection models propose; a reviewer confirms, corrects and adds. What the imagery cannot settle is listed for a ground check.

Dated and credited

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled, never “real‑time”

Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, with a notice after each one.

Confidential by default

Results go only to the contacts you name. Defence sites and signal stations are never mapped, and nothing about your assets is published.

Satellite first, drones under Part 101

Two routes to the picture, and the rules for each

Satellite and your own imagery. A survey starts from your route or boundary file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos you already hold. No aircraft flies and nobody needs to enter the land, so diamond areas, national parks and remote farms are covered the same way as the rest of the route.

Drone detail. Where a stretch needs more detail than satellite imagery shows, a drone survey captures it, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires. In Namibia that means an NCAA RPAS Letter of Approval under NAMCAR Part 101 for each operation, applied for at least 30 days ahead, pilots with NCAA remote pilot certificates, and an RPAS Operator Certificate for any flight beyond visual line of sight, which the NCAA issues only to Namibian persons and companies. Flights over private property need the owner’s permission, and parks, diamond areas and restricted airspace need their own.

Afridrone is working towards the approvals Namibia requires. Every drone proposal names the company that will fly and its approvals, so your team can check them.

The Namibia drone-law guide

The Letter of Approval, the Operator Certificate, remote pilot certificates, height and airfield limits, restricted areas, diamond areas and parks, and a 12-point checklist for anyone commissioning a drone survey, with sources, last reviewed on 27 September 2026.

How it works

From your file to a reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route or boundary, the region and the widths or distances that matter. We agree the bands, the imagery and the deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures, cleared ground and tracks are mapped along the whole route or across the licence area from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or your own orthophotos.

  3. Check up close

    Your own flights, or drone surveys where approvals and landowners allow, cover the stretches that need more detail.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result; each structure is measured, banded and rated, and the report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure in Namibia?

The ones that apply to your asset. Namibian power-line servitude widths are set in each wayleave agreement, road reserves are set by the Roads Ordinance, and the Minerals and Petroleum Acts set 100 m and 300 m consent distances around structures and surveyed erven. Send the widths with the route, or the servitude and licence polygons themselves, and we report each structure’s distance to the line or boundary and the band it falls in, with up to six widths in one survey.

Does a satellite survey need NCAA approval or landowner permission?

No aircraft is flown, so the NCAA’s Part 101 approvals and the landowner permission a drone flight needs do not apply to the satellite work itself; counsel should confirm this for your project. Drone stretches, where you want them, are planned separately and are subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires.

Can you work in diamond restricted areas and national parks?

From satellite imagery, yes, because nobody enters the area. Entering or being in a diamond restricted area needs a Minister’s permit under the Diamond Act, and whether a drone overflight also needs one is unresolved, so the licence holder’s consent and counsel’s view come first. In a national park a drone flight needs approval, and filming needs MEFT approval. See drone law in Namibia.

Can you tell us whether a structure is lawful?

No. We map what stands where and when it first appears in the imagery. Whether a structure is covered by a wayleave, a customary land right, a lease or a permission under the roads ordinances is for your land team, the land board, the traditional authority, the Roads Authority or the courts to decide. The register gives them one dated, located list to work from.

Do you detect copper theft or vandalism?

No. Satellites cannot see theft, vandalism or people. We map land change, such as new structures, fresh digging, cleared ground and new tracks along your lines and routes, so your field teams know where to look first.

Is the register a survey we can register at the Surveyor-General?

No. General plans and diagrams need approval and must be signed by a land surveyor under the Land Survey Act 1993. Our registers are monitoring and planning records built from imagery. They show your surveyor and your wayleave officers where to look, and they support your land, compensation and community processes.

Know what stands on the land before the next farm visit.

Send the line, pipeline or road route, or the licence boundary (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the region, and the widths or distances that apply: those in your wayleave agreements, the road reserve, or the 100 m and 300 m consent distances around planned workings. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
